title: A Daily Pill Just Doubled Pancreatic Cancer Survival. The Audience at ASCO Gave It a Standing Ovation.
excerpt: Daraxonrasib is the first drug ever to meaningfully extend life in metastatic pancreatic cancer — a disease that kills 95 per cent of patients within five years. For South Asians, whose pancreatic cancer rates are climbing, the breakthrough could not be more urgent.
body:
For decades, pancreatic cancer has occupied a uniquely grim position in oncology. It is diagnosed late, resists nearly every treatment, and kills faster than almost any other solid tumour. The five-year survival rate in the United States hovers below 13 per cent. In India, where late-stage diagnosis is even more common, outcomes are worse.

On May 31, researchers at the American Society of Clinical Oncology's annual meeting in Chicago presented results that, for the first time, cracked that wall of futility — and the audience rose to its feet.

## The RASolute 302 Trial

The drug is daraxonrasib, a daily oral pill developed by Revolution Medicines. It targets a family of proteins called RAS, which drive roughly 90 per cent of pancreatic cancers. For forty years, RAS was considered "undruggable" — its molecular surface offered no obvious pocket for a drug to latch onto. Daraxonrasib is a pan-RAS inhibitor: it blocks multiple RAS variants simultaneously, including the KRAS G12 mutations that dominate pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

In the phase III RASolute 302 trial, 500 patients with previously treated metastatic pancreatic cancer were randomly assigned to receive either daraxonrasib or standard chemotherapy. The results were striking. Median overall survival was 13.2 months in the daraxonrasib group versus 6.7 months with chemotherapy — nearly double. Progression-free survival jumped from 1.9 months to 5.6 months. And 31.6 per cent of patients on the drug saw their tumours shrink substantially, compared with 11.2 per cent on chemotherapy.

"It is exciting to see that we may soon be able to help patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer in ways we haven't been able to before," said Brian Wolpin, director of the Hale Family Center for Pancreatic Cancer Research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and the trial's principal investigator.

## A Pill, Not a Drip

One detail that resonated through the ASCO auditorium: daraxonrasib is a daily oral pill. Patients take it at home. Only 1 per cent of participants stopped treatment due to side effects (primarily a skin rash), compared with 11 per cent who discontinued chemotherapy because of fatigue, nausea, and the cumulative toll of infusions. For a disease whose treatment has historically meant spending much of one's remaining life in a clinic, the quality-of-life difference is profound.

The FDA has already granted daraxonrasib Breakthrough Therapy status and allowed patients to enrol in an expanded access programme. A formal approval decision is expected within months.

## Why This Matters for South Asians

Pancreatic cancer incidence is rising across South Asia and among diaspora communities. India recorded an estimated 29,000 new cases in 2022, and the number is climbing as dietary patterns shift and diabetes prevalence — a known risk factor — soars. South Asians in the United States face additional complexity: lower screening rates, later diagnoses, and a persistent gap in clinical trial representation.

The daraxonrasib breakthrough matters here for two reasons. First, KRAS mutations are near-universal in pancreatic adenocarcinoma regardless of ethnicity. The drug's mechanism is not population-specific — it should work across demographics. Second, as an oral medication, it sidesteps the infrastructure bottleneck that makes intravenous chemotherapy difficult to deliver in many parts of India and in rural diaspora communities where oncology centres are sparse.

Researchers are already exploring daraxonrasib as a first-line therapy and in combination with other agents. Tango Therapeutics reported that combining it with their experimental drug vopimetostat shrank tumours in 11 of 12 pancreatic cancer patients in an early trial — 90 per cent had no disease progression after six months.

## Not a Cure — But a Door

Daraxonrasib does not cure pancreatic cancer. Thirteen months is not years, and the disease remains lethal. But this is the first time any drug has meaningfully moved the survival needle in metastatic pancreatic cancer — the first positive phase III trial ever. As Eileen O'Reilly of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center put it: "It's an important step to build on, and the door is now open to lead to other treatments, not just with pancreatic cancer, but other cancers as well."

For the millions of South Asian families who have watched this disease take loved ones with almost no therapeutic options, that open door is not a small thing.

*Sources: The New England Journal of Medicine, Nature Reviews Clinical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Revolution Medicines, USA TODAY, New Scientist*
